author: Dario Amodei
title: Machines of Loving Grace
central_scenario_summary: If safety and geopolitics go right, 'powerful AI' (a 'country of geniuses in a datacenter', smarter than Nobel laureates and runnable as millions of fast copies) could arrive as early as 2026 and, over the following 5-10 years, compress a century of scientific progress: curing most disease, doubling lifespan, and potentially enabling ~20% GDP growth that lets the developing world catch up. On work, comparative advantage keeps humans economically relevant in the short run, but eventually AI becomes so cheap and broadly effective that the current economic setup 'no longer makes sense', requiring new arrangements (possibly UBI). Amodei is relatively optimistic about within-country inequality of access in the developed world, most worried about global inequality, and regards wealth inequality as the hardest unsolved problem.

expertise_erosion.notes: AI is superhuman at expert tasks (science, coding) and eventually ultra-cheap, so expertise rents ultimately compete away; but short-run he stresses human comparative advantage, so the erosion is a long-run outcome.

substitution.notes: Short/medium run: complement via comparative advantage. Long run: full substitution once AI is cheap and broadly effective. Scored mixed for the central 5-10yr window with an explicit long-run shift to strong substitute.

quotes.text: the '10%' expands to continue to employ almost everyone

demand_absorption.notes: Invokes comparative advantage / lump-of-labour fallacy for near-term absorption; but explicitly warns that in the long run most humans may not contribute meaningfully, so absorption eventually breaks down.

quotes.text: the pace I'm describing is probably close to the limits of what society can absorb without extreme turbulence

mobility_adjustment.notes: Deliberately picks a 'tame' pace near the edge of what society can absorb; implies historical-ish adjustment with real turbulence risk. Not a focus of the essay.

quotes.text: markets are typically good at bringing down the cost of high-value technologies over time

rent_concentration.notes: Expects competitive diffusion of access to consumers, especially in the developed world; but flags wealth inequality (as opposed to access) as a harder, unresolved problem in Section 5.

quotes.text: I think it could come as early as 2026 ... focus on what happens in the 5-10 years after that

timeline_years.notes: Powerful AI ~2026; main transformation over the following 5-10 years, i.e. roughly 7-12 years from the 2024 writing. Representative value 10.

quotes.text: I am more optimistic about within-country inequality especially in the developed world

inequality_prediction.notes: FREE TEXT: Amodei is relatively optimistic that within-country inequality of access can be managed in the developed world (markets lower costs; responsive institutions; citizen demand), most concerned about global North-South inequality, and treats wealth inequality (vs. access) as the hardest problem, possibly requiring a new economic settlement (e.g., large UBI) once labor is broadly displaced.
